feedback: If a learner says veins are blue and carry 'dirty' blood, ask whether blood heading TO the lungs is clean or dirty, and which vessel carries it — clarify veins only look blue through skin and deoxygenated blood is dark red, not blue.
If a learner draws the symbolic heart shape on the left, point to the breastbone and describe the real fist-sized muscular pump sitting centrally and tilted slightly left.
activities.intendedInsight: The pulse is the felt heartbeat driving blood through an artery; when the body needs more oxygen the pump speeds up to deliver it, previewing how circulation and breathing work together.
learnerActions: Find the pulse in your wrist or neck and feel it push — this is an artery.
Point out the blue-looking lines on the back of the hand: these are veins seen through the skin (the blood inside is not blue).
Measure your resting pulse by counting beats over a set time.
Do some brisk activity, measure the pulse again, and explain why a faster pump means more oxygen delivered to the body.
Locate where the heart really sits — centrally behind the breastbone, tilted slightly left, about fist-sized — not on the far left and not the symbolic heart shape.
activities.title: Feel your own pump: pulse and the body as manipulative

feedback: If a learner expects the symbolic shape, compare it to the 3D muscle and name the difference.
Keep this to orientation only — return to the flat circuit model to reason about the loops, since the double-loop pathway is easiest to trace as a flat continuous circuit.
activities.intendedInsight: The real heart is a fist-sized muscular pump sitting centrally behind the breastbone, correcting the symbolic 'heart shape on the left' picture.
learnerActions: Briefly view a 3D heart to see it is a chunky central muscle, not a flat symbolic shape, and to see its real position in the chest.
State in your own words where the heart sits and roughly how big it is.
activities.title: Brief 3D orientation: what shape and where the heart really is

feedback: Recall-style sequencing and matching confirm vocabulary but do not by themselves show the flow intuition — pair any gaps with a return to the driveable model.
If a learner can list parts but cannot say what is exchanged where, send them back to trace one drop and narrate the pick-up/drop-off on each leg.
activities.intendedInsight: Sequencing, matching and categorising can confirm the named parts are recalled and connected to the reason the lung trip must come before the body trip; but these checks test recall, so they do not by themselves build the flow intuition.
learnerActions: Put the double-loop stages in order: body → vein → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → body.
Match each vessel type to its function (artery / vein / capillary).
Categorise the four blood components (red cells, white cells, platelets, plasma) by their jobs.
Answer the reasoning prompt: what would go wrong if blood went straight from the body back out to the body again without visiting the lungs first?
activities.title: Consolidate and check: sequence, match, categorise
